nodes.name: Hermes' Lipschitz selector theorem
nodes.statement:
In contrast to this, it was shown in \cite{Hermes} that a Lipschitz continuous
multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ with compact images from $\mathbb{R}^N$ admits a Lipschitz
continuous selector, whose Lipschitz constant does not exceed that of the multifunction;
furthermore, if $F$ is only continuous and of bounded (Jordan) variation, then
it admits a \emph{continuous\/} selector.
nodes.statement_short: A Lipschitz (resp. continuous BV) compact-valued multifunction on $[a,b]$ into $\mathbb{R}^N$ has a Lipschitz (resp. continuous) selector.
assumptions: a Lipschitz continuous multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ with compact images from $\mathbb{R}^N$
if $F$ is only continuous and of bounded (Jordan) variation
conclusions: admits a Lipschitz continuous selector, whose Lipschitz constant does not exceed that of the multifunction

nodes.name: Selection theorem for multifunctions of bounded Jordan variation
nodes.statement:
Changing the compactness arguments to generalized Helly's pointwise selection
principle, it was proved in \cite{JDCS} that a multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ of bounded
Jordan variation with compact images from a Banach space admits a selector,
whose total Jordan variation does not exceed that of $F$ and passes through a
given point in the graph of~$F$.
nodes.statement_short: A compact-valued BV multifunction on $[a,b]$ into a Banach space has a selector through a given graph point with variation at most that of $F$.
assumptions: a multifunction $F$ on $[a,b]$ of bounded Jordan variation with compact images from a Banach space
conclusions: admits a selector, whose total Jordan variation does not exceed that of $F$ and passes through a given point in the graph of~$F$

It follows from (a), (b), and (c) above that $d_H$ is a \emph{metric\/}
(with finite values), called the \emph{Pompeiu-Hausdorff metric}, on the family
$\mbox{bcl}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{bounded closed\/} subsets of $M$ and, in 
particular on the family $\mbox{c}(M)$ of all nonempty \emph{compact\/} subsets of~$M$.
nodes.statement_short: $d_H$ is a metric on nonempty bounded closed sets bcl(M), in particular on nonempty compact sets c(M).

nodes.name: Multifunction
nodes.statement:
A \emph{multifunction\/} (or \emph{set-valued mapping\/}) from a nonempty set $T$
into $M$ is a rule $F$, which assigns to each $t\in T$ a unique subset $F(t)\subset M$;
in symbols, $F:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$, where $\mathcal{P}(M)$ is the power set of $M$
(=\,the family of all subsets of~$M$).
differentia: assigns to each $t\in T$ a unique subset $F(t)\subset M$

nodes.name: Set-valued selector
nodes.statement:
A multifunction $\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$
is said to be a \emph{set-valued selector\/} of $F:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)$ on $T$ provided
$\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$.

nodes.name: Selector (selection)
nodes.statement:
If $\Gamma:T\to M$ is single-valued and $\Gamma(t)\in F(t)$ for all $t\in T$, then
$\Gamma$ is called a \emph{selector\/} (or \emph{selection\/}) of~$F$ on~$T$.

nodes.name: Jordan variation of a multifunction
nodes.statement_short: $V(F,T)$ is the supremum over partitions of sums of $d_H$-distances of consecutive values; $F$ is BV if it is finite.

nodes.name: Theorem A (existence of set-valued selectors of bounded variation)
nodes.statement:
Given $T\subset\mathbb{R}$, $t_0\in T$, $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, and
$F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)<+\infty$, there exists
a set-valued selector $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T$ such that
$d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$ and\/ $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$.
{\rm(}In particular, if $X_0\subset F(t_0)$, the first inequality above gives
$\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$.{\rm)} Furthermore, if $x_0\in M$ and $X_0=\{x_0\}$,
then $\Gamma:T\to M$ may be chosen to be single-valued
and such that $d(x_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le d(x_0,F(t_0))$.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (selectors under bounded directional variation)
nodes.statement:
Suppose $T\subset\mathbb{R}$, $t_0\in T$, $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, and
$F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$.

  \begin{itemize}
\item[{\rm(a)}] Let $a:=\inf T\in T$. If\/ ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, then there exists
a set-valued selector of bounded variation $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
of $F$ on $T$ such that  $d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$,
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$,
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$ $\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$,
and
  \begin{equation} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)-J_a(\Gamma,t_0)\le
  {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T),
  \end{equation}
where $J_a(\Gamma,t_0):=0$ if $t_0=a$, and if $t_0>a$ and $s_0:=\sup T_{[a,t_0)}$,
  \begin{equation} J_a(\Gamma,t_0):=\left\{
  \begin{array}{ccc}
d_H(\Gamma(s_0),\Gamma(t_0)), & \,\,\mbox{if}\,\,\, & s_0\in T_{[a,t_0)},\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\lim_{T\ni t\to s_0-0}\!\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t_0]}),
  & \,\,\mbox{if}\,\,\, & s_0\notin T_{[a,t_0)}.
  \end{array}\right.
  \end{equation}
In particular, if $s_0=t_0$, then $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)=\displaystyle
\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0-0}\!d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma(t_0))$.

\item[{\rm(b)}] Let $b:=\sup T\in T$. If\/ ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, then there exists
a set-valued selector of bounded variation $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
of $F$ on $T$ such that  $d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$,
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{(t_0,b]})\le{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(t_0,b]})$,
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{(-\infty,t_0]})$ $\le{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t_0]})$,
and
  \begin{equation*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)-J_b(\Gamma,t_0)\le
  {\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(t_0,b]})+{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t_0]})\le{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T),
  \end{equation*}
where $J_b(\Gamma,t_0):=0$ if $t_0=b$, and if $t_0<b$ and $s_0:=\inf T_{(t_0,b]}$,
  \begin{equation*}
J_b(\Gamma,t_0):=\left\{
  \begin{array}{ccc}
d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(s_0)), & \,\,\mbox{if}\,\,\, & s_0\in T_{(t_0,b]},\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\lim_{T\ni t\to s_0+0}\!\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,t]}),
  & \,\,\mbox{if}\,\,\, & s_0\notin T_{(t_0,b]}.
  \end{array}\right.
  \end{equation*}
In particular, if $s_0=t_0$, then $J_b(\Gamma,t_0)=\displaystyle
\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0+0}\!d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(t))$.
  \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Zero Jordan variation characterizes constant multifunctions
nodes.statement: By the definition of $\mbox{\rm V}$, $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is constant on $T$.

nodes.name: Zero right variation characterizes nondecreasing multifunctions
nodes.statement:
The definition of~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$
and property (a) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr} imply ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is
\emph{nondecreasing\/} on $T$ in the sense that $F(s)\subset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$
with $s\le t$.
nodes.statement_short: $\overrightarrow{V}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is nondecreasing: $F(s)\subset F(t)$ for $s\le t$.

nodes.name: Zero left variation characterizes nonincreasing multifunctions
nodes.statement:
Similarly, ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$ iff $F$ is \emph{nonincresing\/} on $T$, i.e.,
$F(s)\supset F(t)$ for all $s,t\in T$,~$s\le t$.

nodes.name: Proof of additivity of the right variation
nodes.statement:
Given $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ and
$\eta<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there are $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, a partition $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$
of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m=t$ and a partition $\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$
with $s_0=t$ such that
  \begin{equation} \xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\quad\mbox{and}\quad
\eta<\sum_{j=1}^n e(F(s_{j-1}),F(s_j)).
  \end{equation}
Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{s_j\}_{j=0}^n$ is a partition of $T$, we get, from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})},
$\xi+\eta<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, which, due to the arbitrariness of $\xi$ and $\eta$ as above,
implies the inequality
  \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{equation*}

In order to prove the reverse inequality, let $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary such that
$\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Then, there are $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$
of $T$ such that the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} holds. If $t_m\le t$, then $\pi$ is a
partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$, and if $t\le t_0$, then $\pi$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$,
and so, in the either case, the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} implies
  \begin{equation} \xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}).
  \end{equation}
Now, suppose $t_{k-1}\le t\le t_k$ for some $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$. By the triangle
inequality for~$e$, we have
  \begin{equation} e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t_k))\le e(F(t_{k-1}),F(t))+e(F(t),F(t_k)).
  \end{equation}
Since $\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{k-1}\cup\{t\}$ is a partition of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ and
$\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=k}^m$ is a partition of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$, from the first inequality
in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:xi1})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:kk})}, once again we get \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:x2})}. By the arbitrariness
 of $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$,
\mbox{\rm(\ref{e:x2})} implies
   \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}),
  \end{equation*}
 which was to be proved.
\qed

nodes.name: Variation function
nodes.statement:
Recall that the function $v_F(t)\!:=\!\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\!\in\! T$, is said to be
the {\it var\-i\-a\-tion function\/} of $F$ on~$T$.

nodes.name: Variation functions to the right and to the left
nodes.statement:
We define the \emph{variation function\/} of $F$ to the right (to the left) by
$\ori{v}_F(t):={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$ (by $\ole{v}_F(t):={\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$,
respectively) for all $t\in T$.
nodes.statement_short: $\overrightarrow{v}_F(t)$, $\overleftarrow{v}_F(t)$: directional variations of $F$ on $T\cap(-\infty,t]$.

nodes.name: Variation functions are nondecreasing
nodes.statement:
Clearly, $v_F,\ori{v}_F,\ole{v}_F:T\to[0,+\infty]$ are
\emph{nondecreasing\/} on~$T$.

nodes.name: Abbreviated notation $v$, $\overrightarrow{v}$, $\overleftarrow{v}$
nodes.statement:
If $F$ is clear from the context, we omit the
subscript $F$ and write $v$, $\ori{v}$, and $\ole{v}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (characterization of bounded directional variation)
nodes.statement:
Given $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$, ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ iff
there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
$e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$ moreover,
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)$. {\rm(}A similar assertion holds for ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ if
the inequality is written as $e(F(t),F(s))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$.{\rm)}
nodes.statement_short: $\overrightarrow{V}(F,T)<\infty$ iff $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for a bounded nondecreasing $\varphi$, and then $\overrightarrow{V}(F,T)\le V(\varphi,T)$.
assumptions: Given $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
conclusions: ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ iff there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$
equivalent_conditions: there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $e(F(s),F(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)$ for all $s,t\in T$ with $s\le t;$
nodes.label: l:char

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement:
($\Rightarrow\!$) Let $\ori{v}(t)={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})$, $t\in T$, be the variation
function (to the right) of~$F$. It is nondecreasing on $T$ and bounded:
$\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Given $s,t\in T$, $s\le t$, the additivity
of ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ implies
  \begin{equation*}
e(F(s),F(t))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[s,t]})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})-{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,s]})
=\ori{v}(t)-\ori{v}(s).
  \end{equation*}
It remains to set $\varphi:=\ori{v}$.

($\!\Leftarrow$) Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ be a partition of $T$.
Since $t_{i-1}\le t_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,m$, by the assumption we get
  \begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^me(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))&\le\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\varphi(t_i)-\varphi(t_{i-1})\bigr)
  =\varphi(t_m)-\varphi(t_0)\\
&\le\sup_{t\in T}\varphi(t)-\inf_{s\in T}\varphi(s)=\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)<+\infty.
  \end{align*}
It remains to take the supremum over all partitions $\pi$ of $T$.
\qed
nodes.statement_short: ($\Rightarrow$) take $\varphi$ the right variation function, using additivity; ($\Leftarrow$) telescoping sum over any partition.

nodes.name: Total boundedness of the image fails under directional bounds
nodes.statement:
It is known (\cite[1.23]{Var}, \cite[Lemma~11]{MZ}) that if $F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$
and $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$, then the image $F(T):=\bigcup_{t\in T}F(t)$ is a
\emph{totally bounded\/} (hence separable) subset of~$M$ (if, in addition, $(M,d)$ is
complete, then the closure of $F(T)$ in $M$ is compact). However,
condition $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ cannot be replaced neither by
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ nor by ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty$ (see Example~\ref{ex:5.5}).
nodes.statement_short: BV implies totally bounded image $F(T)$, but finiteness of only one directional variation does not.
nodes.label: p:7

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity of the Jordan variation
nodes.statement:
If a sequence $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$
\emph{converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$} to $F$ (i.e.,
$d_H(F_n(t),F(t))\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $t\in T$), then
  \begin{equation} \mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(F_n,T).
  \end{equation}
This property is known as the (sequential) \emph{lower semicontinuity\/} of~$\mbox{\rm V}$
(in the first variable) for metric space valued functions; cf. \cite[Proposition~2.1(V7)]{MatSb}.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise convergence in $(c(M),d_H)$ gives $V(F,T)\le\liminf V(F_n,T)$.
assumptions: a sequence $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ \emph{converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$} to $F$

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity of directional variations
nodes.statement: We assert that \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vsem})} is valid for ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ in place of $\mbox{\rm V}$, as well.

nodes.name: Proof of lower semicontinuity of the right variation
nodes.statement_short: Excess is continuous under $d_H$-convergence; pass to liminf in partition sums, then take sup over partitions.

nodes.name: Limit equalities for the Jordan variation
nodes.statement:
The following equalities are known (\cite{Var,JDCS}) for (multi)functions $F$ on $T$
with values in a metric space (in particular in $\mbox{c}(M)$):
  \begin{align}
&\mbox{if $s\!=\!\sup T\!\in\!\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ and $s\!\notin\! T$, then
  $\displaystyle\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!=\!\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]});$} \\
&\mbox{if \,$i\!=\!\inf T\!\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ \,and $i\!\notin\! T$, then
  $\displaystyle\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\!=\!\lim_{T\ni t\to i}\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)}).$} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: If $\sup T\notin T$ ($\inf T\notin T$), $V(F,T)$ is the limit of variations over $T\cap(-\infty,t]$ ($T\cap[t,\infty)$).

nodes.name: Limit equalities for directional variations
nodes.statement: We are going to show that these assertions hold for ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ as well.

nodes.name: Proof of (3.6) for the right variation
nodes.statement:
Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing on $T$, the limit on the right in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ttos})} (with $\mbox{\rm V}$
replaced by~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$) exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and is equal to $\sup_{t\in T}\ori{v}(t)$.
Given $t\in T$, we have $T_{(-\infty,t]}\subset T$, and so, $\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$,
which implies $\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. Conversely, given $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$
with $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, there are $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T$
(and so, \mbox{$t_0\le t_1\le\dots\le t_{m-1}\le t_m<s$}) such that
  \begin{equation*}
\xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))\le\ori{v}(t_m)\le\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t).
  \end{equation*}
Passing to the limit as $\xi\to{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$, we get ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le\lim_{T\ni t\to s}\ori{v}(t)$.
\qed
nodes.statement_short: Monotone limit of the right variation function, bounded above trivially and below via near-optimal partitions.

nodes.name: Left and right limit points
nodes.statement:
We say that $t\in\mathbb{R}$ is a \emph{left\/} (\emph{right\/}) \emph{limit point\/} of~$T$ if
$T_{(t-\varepsilon,t)}\ne\varnothing$ (respectively, $T_{(t,t+\varepsilon)}\ne\varnothing$) for all $\varepsilon>0$.

nodes.name: Left and right isolated points
nodes.statement:
A point $t\in T$, which is not a left (or right) limit point of $T$, is called the \emph{left\/}
(or \emph{right\/}) \emph{isolated point\/} of~$T$.

nodes.name: Jump formulas for the variation function
nodes.statement_short: For BV $F$, the variation function jumps at a limit point by the left/right jump of $F$.
assumptions: $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)<+\infty$

nodes.name: Left and right jumps
nodes.statement:
The second limit in the right-hand side of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:VFtm})} (of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:VF+0})}) is known as
the \emph{left\/} (\emph{right\/}, respectively) \emph{jump\/} of $F$ at~$t$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (jump formulas for directional variation functions)
nodes.statement_short: Directional variation functions jump at limit points by the limsup of the appropriately ordered excess.
assumptions: If $t\in T$ is a left limit point of $T$
If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$
nodes.label: l:jumps

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement:
We concentrate on ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) and ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$),
making only remarks on ($\ole{\mbox{\rm a}}$) and ($\ole{\mbox{\rm b}}$).

($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$)
First, we prove inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$).
By the additivity of ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$, given $s\in T$ with $s<t$, we have
  \begin{equation*}
\ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ori{v}(s)+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[s,t]})=\ori{v}(t).
  \end{equation*}
Since $\ori{v}$ is nondecreasing and bounded on $T$ (by ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$), and $t$ is a left
limit point of $T$, the left limit $\ori{v}(t-0)$ exists in $[0,+\infty)$ and is equal to
$\sup\{\ori{v}(s):s\in T,s<t\}$. Inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) follows
now from the properties of the limit superior as $T\!\ni\! s\!\to\! t\!-\!0$, since
the right-hand side in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$) is equal to
  \begin{equation*}
\lim_{T\ni s\to t-0}\!\ori{v}(s)\!+\!\limsup_{T\ni s\to t-0}\!e(F(s),F(t))\!=\!
\limsup_{T\ni s\to t-0}\!\bigl(\ori{v}(s)\!+\!e(F(s),F(t))\bigr)\le\ori{v}(t).
  \end{equation*}

Now we show that inequality $\le$ holds in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm a}}$). By the definition
of $\ori{v}(t)$, which is finite, for any $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$, $\xi<\ori{v}(t)$, there are $m\in\mathbb{N}$
and a partition $\pi=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m\cup\{t\}$ of $T_{(-\infty,t]}$ with $t_m<t$
such that
  \begin{equation*}
\xi<\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i))+e(F(t_m),F(t)).
  \end{equation*}
Given $s\in T_{(t_m,t)}$, the triangle inequality for $e$ implies
  \begin{equation*}
e(F(t_m),F(t))\le e(F(t_m),F(s))+e(F(s),F(t)),
  \end{equation*}
and so, $\xi<\ori{v}(s)+e(F(s),F(t))$. Passing to the limit superior as
$T\ni s\to t-0$, we get
  \begin{equation*}
\xi\le\ori{v}(t-0)+\limsup_{T\ni s\to t-0}e(F(s),F(t)).
  \end{equation*}
It remains to take into account the arbitrariness of $\xi<\ori{v}(t)$.

\smallbreak
($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$)
In order to prove inequality $\ge$ in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$), we make use of the
additivity of ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ to get
  \begin{equation*}
\ori{v}(t)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ori{v}(t)+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,s]})=\ori{v}(s)\quad
\mbox{for all $s\in T_{(t,+\infty)}$.}
  \end{equation*}
Now, it suffices to pass to the limit superior as $T\ni  s\to t+0$.

To show inequality $\le$ in ($\ori{\mbox{\rm b}}$), we apply the additivity property
of ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ several times. To begin with, note that
  \begin{equation} {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)-\ori{v}(t).
  \end{equation}
Given $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\xi<{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})$, there exist $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and a
partition $\{t\}\cup\{t_i\}_{i=0}^m$ of $T_{[t,+\infty)}$ with $t<t_0$ such that
  \begin{equation*}
\xi<e(F(t),F(t_0))+\sum_{i=1}^m e(F(t_{i-1}),F(t_i)).
  \end{equation*}
Since, for any $s\!\in\! T_{(t,t_0)}$, $e(F(t),F(t_0))\!\le\! e(F(t),F(s))\!+\!e(F(s),F(t_0))$,
we~find
  \begin{align*}
\xi+\ori{v}(t_m)-{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\le\xi&<e(F(t),F(s))+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[s,t_m]})\\[2pt]
&=e(F(t),F(s))+\ori{v}(t_m)-\ori{v}(s),
  \end{align*}
and so, $\ori{v}(s)\le({\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)-\xi)+e(F(t),F(s))$. Passing to the limit superior as
$T\ni s\to t+0$, we get
  \begin{equation*}
\ori{v}(t+0)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)-\xi+\limsup_{T\ni s\to t+0}e(F(t),F(s)).
  \end{equation*}
It remains to let $\xi$ tend to the value \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:tin})}.

\smallbreak
($\ole{\mbox{\rm a}}$), ($\ole{\mbox{\rm b}}$)
Here we note only that, by the additivity of ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$,
  \begin{align*}
\ole{v}(s)+e(F(t),F(s))\le\ole{v}(s)+{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[s,t]})=\ole{v}(t)\quad
  \forall\,s\in T_{(-\infty,t)},\\[2pt]
\ole{v}(t)+e(F(s),F(t))\le\ole{v}(t)+{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,s]})=\ole{v}(s)\quad
  \forall\,s\in T_{(t,+\infty)},
  \end{align*}
respectively.
\qed
nodes.statement_short: Each jump formula: $\ge$ from additivity plus limsup, $\le$ from near-optimal partitions and the triangle inequality for $e$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3 (one-sided directional variations at limit points)
nodes.statement:
If $t\in T$ is a left limit point of $T$, then
  \begin{itemize}
\item[${\rm(\ori{\mbox{\rm a}})}$]
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})\!=\!{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})\!+\!\displaystyle
  \limsup_{T\ni s\to t-0}e(F(s),F(t))$ \,if \,\,${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty;$
\item[${\rm(\ole{\mbox{\rm a}})}$]
${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t]})\!=\!{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t)})\!+\!\displaystyle
  \limsup_{T\ni s\to t-0}e(F(t),F(s))$ \,if \,\,${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty.$
  \end{itemize}

If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$, then
  \begin{itemize}
\item[${\rm(\ori{\mbox{\rm b}})}$]
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\!=\!{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(t,+\infty)})\!+\!\displaystyle
  \limsup_{T\ni s\to t+0}e(F(t),F(s))$ \,if \,\,${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\!<\!+\infty;$
\item[${\rm(\ole{\mbox{\rm b}})}$]
${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t,+\infty)})\!=\!{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(t,+\infty)})\!+\!\displaystyle
  \limsup_{T\ni s\to t+0}e(F(s),F(t))$ \,if \,\,${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty.$
  \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Directional variation over $T\cap(-\infty,t]$ equals that over $T\cap(-\infty,t)$ plus the limsup excess jump (and symmetrically on the right).
assumptions: If $t\in T$ is a left limit point of $T$
If $t\in T$ is a right limit point of $T$
nodes.label: l:opej

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 2 with the limit equalities (3.6)-(3.7) and additivity.

nodes.name: Modulus of variation
nodes.statement_short: $\nu_k(F,T)$: sup of sums of $d_H(F(s_i),F(t_i))$ over $k$ nonoverlapping ordered pairs.

nodes.name: Modulus of variation converges to the Jordan variation
nodes.statement:
The general case of metric space valued functions was considered in \cite{JMAA05},
whence we know that $\nu_k(F,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and
$\nu_k(F,T)\to\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)$ as $k\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Theorem B (pointwise selection principle)
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of multifunctions
$F_n:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that\/
{\rm(a)} $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$
\footnote{Equality $\mu_k=o(k)$ means as usual that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mu_k/k=0$.},
and\/ {\rm(b)}~the closure in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of the set $\{F_n(t):n\in\mathbb{N}\}$
is compact for all $t\in T$. Then $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ admits a subsequence,
which converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a multifunction
$F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\nu_k(F,T)=o(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: A sequence with $\limsup_n\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$ and pointwise relatively compact values has a pointwise convergent subsequence.
assumptions: $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of multifunctions $F_n:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(F_n,T)=o(k)$
the closure in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ of the set $\{F_n(t):n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is compact for all $t\in T$
conclusions: $\{F_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ admits a subsequence, which converges in $\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a multifunction $F:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that $\nu_k(F,T)=o(k)$
nodes.label: t:B

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
We prove only item (a), item (b) being proved similarly with corresponding modifications
(`to the left'). We divide the proof into six steps for clarity.
Recall that $a=\inf T\in T$, and we set $b:=\sup T$.
In the first four steps, we prove the theorem in the case when $t_0=a$
and $b\in T$ (so that $T\subset[t_0,b]$ is bounded), in step~5---when $t_0=a$ and
$b\notin T$, and in step~6---when $t_0\!>\!a$ and $T$ is arbitrary.
We employ several ideas from \cite{JMAA,MatSb}, \cite[Sections~5,~10]{Sovae}.

\smallbreak
{\it Step~1}. Suppose $T\subset[t_0,b]$ and $t_0,b\in T$. Since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$ is finite
and the variation function of $F$ to the right $\ori{v}:T\to[0,+\infty)$ is nondecreasing
on~$T$, the set of its points of discontinuity on $T$ is at most countable. Denote by
$T_F$ the set of points $t\in T$, which are left limit points of $T$ such that
$\ori{v}(t)=\ori{v}(t-0)$. It follows that $T\setminus T_F$ is at most countable and,
by Lemma~\ref{l:jumps}${\rm(\ori{\mbox{\rm a}})}$,
  \begin{equation} \mbox{if $t\in T_F$, then $e(F(s),F(t))\to0$ as $T\ni s\to t-0$.}
  \end{equation}
Furthermore, the set $T_0$ of left isolated points of $T$
(i.e., $t\in T$ such that $T_{(t-\varepsilon,t)}=\varnothing$ for some $\varepsilon>0$) is also at most
countable (in fact, the intervals of ``emptiness from the left'', corresponding to
different left isolated points of $T$, are disjoint, and each such interval contains
a rational number). Let $Q$ denote an at most countable dense subset of $T$. We set
  \begin{equation*}
S\!:=\{t_0,b\}\cup(T\setminus T_F)\cup T_0\cup Q
  \end{equation*}
and note that $S\subset T$ is dense in $T$ and at most countable. With no loss
of generality we may assume that $S$ is countable, say, $S=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^\infty$.
Given $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the set $\pi_n=\{t_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1}\cup\{b\}$ is a partition of $T$.
Ordering the points in $\pi_n$ in ascending order and denoting the resulting (ordered)
partition of $T$ by $\pi_n=\{t_i^n\}_{i=0}^n$, we get
  \begin{eqnarray}
&\mbox{$t_0=t_0^n<t_1^n<\dots<t_{n-1}^n<t_n^n=b$, \,and}& \\[2pt]
&\mbox{$\forall\,t\in S$ $\exists\,n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in\pi_n$
  for all $n\ge n_0$.}& \end{eqnarray}

{\it Step~2}. Let us construct an approximating sequence for the desired set-valued
selector of $F$. In order to do this, we need the following observation from
\cite[assertion (10.2)]{Sovae}: given $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$,
  \begin{equation} \mbox{there is $Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y'\subset Y$ and
$d_H(X,Y')\le e(X,Y)$.}
  \end{equation}
In fact, it suffices to define $Y'$ as the \emph{metric projection\/} of $X$ onto~$Y$:
  \begin{equation} Y'=\mbox{\rm Pr}_Y X:=\{y\in Y:\mbox{there is $x\in X$ such that $d(x,y)=d(x,Y)$}\}.
  \end{equation}

First, given $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we define sets $Y_i^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$, $i=0,1,\dots,n$,
inductively as follows. Setting $X=X_0$ and $Y=F(t_0)$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, we choose
$Y_0:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that $Y_0\subset F(t_0)$ and
$d_H(X_0,Y_0)\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$. We put $Y_0^n:=Y_0$ (for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$).
Now, suppose $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and the set $Y_{i-1}^n\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$Y_{i-1}^n\subset F(t_{i-1}^n)$ is already chosen. Then, we put $X=Y_{i-1}^n$
and $Y=F(t_i^n)$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})} and pick $Y_i^n:=Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)$ and
  \begin{equation} d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)\le e(Y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))\le e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n)).
  \end{equation}

The approximating sequence $\Gamma_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, is defined as
a sequence of set-valued step functions of the form (cf. \cite[equation~(10.3)]{Sovae}):
  \begin{align}
\Gamma_n(t_i^n)&:=Y_i^n\quad\mbox{for all \,$i=0,1,\dots,n;$} \\[2pt]
\Gamma_n(t)&:=Y_{i-1}^n\,\,\,\mbox{for all $t\in T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$
  and $i=1,\dots,n$} \end{align}
(if $T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)=\varnothing$, then $\Gamma_n$ is left undefined
on $(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$). Clearly,
  \begin{equation*}
\Gamma_n(t_0)=\Gamma_n(t_0^n)=Y_0^n=Y_0\subset F(t_0)\quad
\mbox{for all \,$n\in\mathbb{N}$.}
  \end{equation*}
Moreover, by the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Yin})}, we have
  \begin{align}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_n,T)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_n,T\cap[t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n])
  =\sum_{i=1}^n d_H(Y_{i-1}^n,Y_i^n)\nonumber\\
&\le\sum_{i=1}^n e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n))\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)
  \quad\mbox{for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.} \end{align}

{\it Step~3}. Let us show that $\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ satisfies the assumptions
of Theorem~\ref{t:B}. By virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:gn})}, we get
  \begin{equation*}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\nu_k(\Gamma_n,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\mathbb{N}$,}
  \end{equation*}
and so, condition (a) in Theorem~\ref{t:B} is satisfied. Now, we verify condition~(b).

If $t\in S$, then, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})}, there is $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $t\in\pi_n$ for
all $n\ge n_0$. So, for each $n\ge n_0$ there is $i=i(t,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ such that
$t=t_i^n$. The definition of $\Gamma_n$ implies
  \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=\Gamma_n(t_i^n)=Y_i^n\subset F(t_i^n)=F(t)\quad
\mbox{for all \,$n\ge n_0$.}
  \end{equation}
In other words, $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=n_0}^\infty\subset\mbox{c}(F(t))$. Since
$F(t)$ is a compact subset of $M$, it follows from \cite[II.1.4]{CV} that
$\mbox{c}(F(t))$ is a compact subset of $\mbox{c}(M)$, which implies the desired
property for $\{F_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$.

Suppose now that $t\in T\setminus S$. We have $t\in T_F\cap(t_0,b)$, i.e., by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:FsFt})},
  \begin{equation} e(F(s),F(t))\to0\quad\mbox{as}\quad T_{(t_0,b)}\ni s\to t-0,
  \end{equation}
where $t$ is a left limit point of $T$, and so,
there is a sequence $\tau_k\in T$, $\tau_k<t$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, such that $\tau_k\to t$
as $k\to\infty$. Since $S$ is dense in $T$, given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there is $s_k\in S$ such
that $|s_k-\tau_k|<t-\tau_k$, which implies $s_k<t$, and $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$.
From \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})}, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ choose a number $n_0(k)\in\mathbb{N}$ (depending
also on~$t$) such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$. We may assume (arguing
inductively) that the sequence $\{n_0(k)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ is strictly increasing.
Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n\ge n_0(k)$, since $s_k\in\pi_n$, there is a number
$j(k,n)\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n$ and, since $s_k<t$, there is
(unique) $i(k,n)\in\{j(k,n),\dots,n-1\}$ such that
  \begin{equation} s_k=t_{j(k,n)}^n\le t_{i(k,n)}^n<t<t_{i(k,n)+1}^n.
  \end{equation}
By \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})}, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:re})}, and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})}, we find
  \begin{equation} \Gamma_n(t)=Y_{i(k,n)}^n\subset F(t_{i(k,n)}^n)\quad\mbox{for all \,$k\in\mathbb{N}$
  \,and \,$n\ge n_0(k)$.}
  \end{equation}
Setting $n:=n_0(k)$ and $p_k:=t_{i(k,n_0(k))}^{n_0(k)}$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we have
$\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t)\subset F(p_k)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$, where, by virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})}
and property $s_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$,
  \begin{equation} \mbox{$p_k<t$ \,and \,$p_k\to t$ \,as \,$k\to\infty$.}
  \end{equation}
Applying \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})}, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ pick $Y_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$Y_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and
  \begin{equation} d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},Y_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{n_0(k)},F(t))\le e(F(p_k),F(t)).
  \end{equation}
It follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:*7})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:pkt})} that the right-hand side in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gok})} tends
to zero as $k\to\infty$. By the compactness of $\mbox{c}(F(t))$, we may assume
(passing to a subsequence of $\{Y_k(t)\}_{k=1}^\infty$ if necessary) that
$d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for some $Y(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$Y(t)\subset F(t)$. Thus,
  \begin{equation*}
d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y(t))\!\le\! d_H(\Gamma_{n_0(k)}(t),Y_k(t))
  \!+\!d_H(Y_k(t),Y(t))\!\to\!0\quad\mbox{as \,$k\!\to\!\infty$,}
  \end{equation*}
and so, (a subsequence of) the subsequence $\{\Gamma_{n_0(k)}\}_{k=1}^\infty$
of $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges in $\mbox{c}(M)$. This finishes
the proof of compactness of $\ov{\{\Gamma_n(t)\}_{n=1}^\infty}$ (the closure
being taken in $\mbox{c}(M)$).

\smallbreak
{\it Step~4}. By Theorem~\ref{t:B}, there are a subsequence of
$\{\Gamma_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, which we denote by
$\{\Gamma_{l(n)}\}_{n=1}^\infty$ with strictly increasing $l:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, and
a multifunction $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$d_H(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),\Gamma(t))\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $t\in T$.

Let us show that $\Gamma$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$. It is clear from
\mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:op})} that $\Gamma(t_0)=Y_0\subset F(t_0)$, and so (cf. Step~2),
  \begin{equation} d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0)).
  \end{equation}

If $t\in S$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:noN})} implies $t\in\pi_n$ for some $n_0=n_0(t)\in\mathbb{N}$ and all $n\ge n_0$.
Since $l(n)\ge l(n_0)\ge n_0$ for $n\ge n_0$, it follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Gat})} that
$\Gamma_{l(n)}(t)\subset F(t)$, and so
(cf.\ properties (a) and (b) of $e$ in Section~\ref{s:mr}),
  \begin{align*}
e(\Gamma(t),F(t))&\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))
  +e(\Gamma_{l(n)}(t),F(t)) \\[2pt]
&=e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))\le d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{l(n)}(t))
  \to0\quad\mbox{as \,$n\to\infty$.}
  \end{align*}
This gives $e(\Gamma(t),F(t))=0$ implying $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$.

Now suppose that $t\in T\setminus S$. Given $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $n_0(k)$ be the number
(also depending on $t$) from Step~3 such that $s_k\in\pi_n$ for all $n\ge n_0(k)$.
Hence, assertions \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})} still hold. Setting
$n=N(k):=l(n_0(k))\ge n_0(k)$ and $q_k:=t_{i(k,N(k))}^{N(k)}$ in
\mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ijkn})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Fikn})}, we find $\Gamma_{N(k)}\subset F(q_k)$, where
$q_k<t$, and $q_k\to t$ as $k\to\infty$. For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$, thanks to \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:proj})},
let $Z_k(t)\in\mbox{c}(M)$ be such that $Z_k(t)\subset F(t)$ and
  \begin{equation*}
d_H(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))\le e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),F(t))\le e(F(q_k),F(t)).
  \end{equation*}
Noting that $e(Z_k(t),F(t))=0$, we get
  \begin{equation*}
e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\le e(\Gamma(t),\Gamma_{N(k)}(t))
  +e(\Gamma_{N(k)}(t),Z_k(t))+e(Z_k(t),F(t))
  \end{equation*}
with the right-hand side tending to zero as $n\!\to\!\infty$. Hence
\mbox{$e(\Gamma(t),F(t))\!=\!0$}, and so, $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$.
Thus, we have shown that $\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$.

The lower semicontinuity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:gn})} imply
  \begin{equation*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_{l(n)},T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{equation*}
Since $T_{[a,t_0)}\!=\!\varnothing$ (recall that $t_0\!=\!a$),
$T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\!=\!T_{[t_0,b]}\!=\!T$, and \mbox{$J_a(\Gamma,t_0)\!=\!0$},
this proves Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) in the case when $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T\in T$.

\smallbreak
{\it Remark}. Note that if $X_0\subset F(t_0)$, we have, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xo})},
$\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$.

\smallbreak
{\it Step~5}. Suppose $t_0=a$ and $b=\sup T\notin T$, so that
$T_{[a,t_0)}\!=\!\varnothing$, $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\!=\!T$, and $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)=0$.
Pick an increasing sequence $\{t_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\subset T$ such that
$t_k\to b$ as $k\to\infty$. Noting that ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,t_1]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$
and applying Steps 1--4 to $F$ on $T_{[t_0,t_1]}$, we get a set-valued selector
$\Gamma_0:T_{[t_0,t_1]}\to\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_0,t_1]}$ such that
  \begin{equation*}
d_H(X_0,\Gamma_0(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\mbox{and}\quad
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_0,T_{[t_0,t_1]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,t_1]}).
  \end{equation*}
Inductively, if $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and a set-valued selector $\Gamma_{k-1}$ of $F$ on
$T_{[t_{k-1},t_k]}$ is already chosen, we note that
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, again apply Steps 1--4, and find
a set-valued selector $\Gamma_k$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}$ such that
$\Gamma_k(t_k)=\Gamma_{k-1}(t_k)$ and
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_k,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})$.
Since $t_k\to b$ as $k\to\infty$, and $b\notin T$, we have
$T=\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}$, so if $t\in T$ and $t\in T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]}$
for some $k\in\{0\}\cup\mathbb{N}$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_k(t)$. Clearly,
$\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ is a well-defined set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$,
inequality \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xo})} holds, and, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ttos})} and the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ and~${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$,
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{(-\infty,t_n]})
  =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_k,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})\\
&\le\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_k,t_{k+1}]})
  =\lim_{n\to\infty}{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{(-\infty,t_n]})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{align*}

{\it Step~6}. Finally, suppose $t_0>a$. Since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$ and
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$ do not exceed ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$, and $X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$,
we apply Steps 1--5 twice: first, to $F$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ with arbitrary
$K_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$ in order to obtain a set-valued selector $\Gamma_1$ of $F$
on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ such that
  \begin{equation*}
d_H(K_0,\Gamma_1(a))\le e(K_0,F(a))\quad\mbox{and}\quad
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)}),
  \end{equation*}
and, second, to $F$ on $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ in order to obtain a set-valued selector
$\Gamma_2$ of $F$ on $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ such that
  \begin{equation*}
d_H(X_0,\Gamma_2(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\mbox{and}\quad
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_2,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)}).
  \end{equation*}
Given $t\in T$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_1(t)$ if $t\in T_{[a,t_0)}$, and
$\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_2(t)$ if $t\in T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$.
\linebreak
Clearly, $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$, inequality
\mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xo})} holds, $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$, and
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})$. Furthermore,
since ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}$ is additive, the second inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:s1t0})} holds (recall that $a=\min T$):
  \begin{align*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})&\le
  {\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0]})+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})=\\[2pt]
&={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,+\infty)})={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{align*}

Let us prove the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:s1t0})}.

Suppose $s_0\in T_{[a,t_0)}$. Hence $s_0=\max T_{[a,t_0)}<t_0$, and so,
$T_{[a,t_0)}=T_{[a,s_0]}$ and $T_{[s_0,t_0]}=\{s_0,t_0\}$ (two-point set).
By the additivity of~$\mbox{\rm V}$,
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0]})&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,s_0]})+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[s_0,t_0]})
  \\[2pt]
&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})+d_H(\Gamma_1(s_0),\Gamma_2(t_0)),
  \end{align*}
which implies
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0]})+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\\[2pt]
&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})+d_H(\Gamma_1(s_0),\Gamma_2(t_0))
  +\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_2,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\\[2pt]
&\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})+d_H(\Gamma(s_0),\Gamma(t_0))+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)}).
  \end{align*}
This proves inequality \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:s1t0})} with 
$J_a(\Gamma,t_0)=d_H(\Gamma(s_0),\Gamma(t_0))$ from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:J})}.

Now, suppose $s_0\notin T_{[a,t_0)}$. Note that $s_0$ is a left limit point of
$T_{[a,s_0)}$ (and so, of  $T_{[a,t_0)}$ and $T$ as well).
In fact, by the definition of $s_0$, $t<s_0$
for all $t\in T_{[a,s_0)}$, and, given $\varepsilon>0$, there is $t_\varepsilon\in T_{[a,s_0)}$
such that $s_0-\varepsilon<t_\varepsilon$. Hence $s_0-\varepsilon<t_\varepsilon<s_0$, i.e.,
$T_{[a,s_0)}\cap(s_0-\varepsilon,s_0)\ne\varnothing$ (and a fortiori $T\cap(s_0-\varepsilon,s_0)\ne\varnothing$).

Let us show that the limit in the right-hand side of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:J})} exists in $[0,+\infty)$.
Since $\Gamma=\Gamma_1$ on $T_{[a,t_0)}$ and
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$, given $t,t'\in T_{[a,s_0)}$
with $t\le t'$, the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ implies (note again that $a=\min T$)
  \begin{align*}
0&\le\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t_0]})-\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t',t_0]})=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t']})
  \\[2pt]
&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{(-\infty,t']})-\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{(-\infty,t]}).
  \end{align*}
By \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ttos})}, the right-hand side here tends to
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,s_0)})-\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,s_0)})=0$ as $T\ni t,t'\to s_0-0$,
and so, Cauchy's criterion yields the existence of the~limit.

Applying the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$ once again, we get
  \begin{equation} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0]})=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t]})+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t_0]})
\quad\mbox{for all \,$t\in T_{[a,s_0)}$.}
  \end{equation}
Noting that $s_0\notin T_{[a,t_0)}$ implies $T_{[a,s_0)}=T_{[a,t_0)}$, by virtue
of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:ttos})}, the limit of the first term in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:star})} as $T\ni t\to s_0-0$ is equal to
  \begin{align*}
\lim_{T\ni t\to s_0-0}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t]})&=
  \lim_{T\ni t\to s_0-0}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{(-\infty,t]})=
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,s_0)})\\[2pt]
&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)}).
  \end{align*}
Taking into account \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:J})}, it follows from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:star})} that
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0]})+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\\[2pt]
&=\lim_{T\ni t\to s_0-0}\!\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t]})+
  \lim_{T\ni t\to s_0-0}\!\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t_0]})+
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_2,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\\
&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_1,T_{[a,t_0)})+J_a(\Gamma,t_0)+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_2,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})
  \\[2pt]
&\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})+J_a(\Gamma,t_0)+{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)}).
  \end{align*}
This proves the first inequality in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:s1t0})}.

It remains to show that if $s_0=t_0$, then $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)$ is the left jump of
$\Gamma$ at~$t_0$.\linebreak
Noting that, by the additivity of $\mbox{\rm V}$,
  \begin{equation*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t_0]})=\ori{v}(t_0)-\ori{v}(t)\quad\mbox{for all \,$t\in T_{[a,t_0)}$,}
  \end{equation*}
and, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:VFtm})},
  \begin{equation*}
\ori{v}(t_0)=\ori{v}(t_0-0)+\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0-0}d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma(t_0)),
  \end{equation*}
and passing to the limit as $T\ni t\to t_0-0$, we get
  \begin{align*}
J_a(\Gamma,t_0)&=\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0-0}\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t,t_0]})
  =\ori{v}(t_0)-\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0-0}\ori{v}(t)\\
&=\ori{v}(t_0-0)+\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0-0}d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma(t_0))-\ori{v}(t_0-0)\\
&=\lim_{T\ni t\to t_0-0}d_H(\Gamma(t),\Gamma(t_0)).
  \end{align*}

This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:BV}.
\qed
nodes.statement_short: Build set-valued step-function approximations via metric projections along dense partitions, extract a pointwise limit by Theorem B, then glue pieces for general $T$ and $t_0$. Key step: compactness of $\{\Gamma_n(t)\}$ at points outside the dense set via left-continuity of the excess.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A from Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Setting $T_+=T_{[t_0,+\infty)}$ and $T_-=T_{(-\infty,t_0]}$, we have
  \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_+)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_+)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)\quad\mbox{and}\quad
  {\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_-)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_-)\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T).
  \end{equation*}
Noting that $t_0\in T_+\cap T_-$ and applying Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) to $F$ on $T_+$
and Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(b) to $F$ on $T_-$, we obtain a set-valued selector
$\Gamma_+:T_+\to\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_+$ and a set-valued selector
$\Gamma_-:T_-\to\mbox{c}(M)$ of $F$ on $T_-$ such that
  \begin{eqnarray*}
&d_H(X_0,\Gamma_+(t_0))\!\le\! e(X_0,F(t_0))\quad\!\mbox{and}\quad\!
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_+,T_+)\!\le\!{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_+),&\\[2pt]
&d_H(\Gamma_+(t_0),\Gamma_-(t_0))\!\le\! e(\Gamma_+(t_0),F(t_0))\!=\!0\quad\!
  \mbox{and}\!\quad\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_-,T_-)\!\le\!{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_-).&
  \end{eqnarray*}
Noting that $\Gamma_-(t_0)=\Gamma_+(t_0)$, we set $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_+(t)$
if $t\in T_+$, and $\Gamma(t):=\Gamma_-(t)$ if $t\in T_-\setminus\{t_0\}$.
Clearly, $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$,
$d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))$ and, by the additivity of~$\mbox{\rm V}$,
  \begin{align}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_+)+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_-)=
  \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_+,T_+)+\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_-,T_-)\nonumber\\[1pt]
&\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_+)+{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_-) \\[2pt]
&\le\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_+)+\mbox{\rm V}(F,T_-)=\mbox{\rm V}(F,T). \nonumber
  \end{align}
This finishes the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:A}. Note that we have shown a little
bit more: inequality \mbox{\rm(\ref{RR})} holds provided ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_+)$ and ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_-)$ are finite.
\qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1(a) on $T\cap[t_0,\infty)$ and 1(b) on $T\cap(-\infty,t_0]$, glue at $t_0$, and bound by additivity.

nodes.name: Single-valued selectors of bounded variation
nodes.statement:
If $X_0=\{x_0\}\subset M$, a (single-valued) selector of bounded var\-i\-a\-tion
$\Gamma:T\!\to\! M$ of $F$ on $T$ may be chosen such that
\mbox{$d(x_0,\Gamma(t_0))\!\le\! d(x_0,F(t_0))$} and satisfying the rest of assertions
in (a) and (b) of Theorem~\ref{t:BV} (if we replace $d_H$ by $d$ everywhere).
In order to see this, it suffices to pick only one element in the corresponding metric
projection. So (cf. Step~2 in the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:BV}),
choose $y_0\in F(t_0)$ such that $d(x_0,y_0)=d(x_0,F(t_0))$, set $y_0^n:=y_0$,
and if $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and elements $y_{i-1}^n\in F(t_{i-1}^n)$ are already chosen,
pick \mbox{$y_i^n\in F(t_i^n)$} such that $d(y_{i-1}^n,y_i^n)=d(y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))$.
Define $\Gamma_n:T\to M$ (as in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:4+})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:re})}) by
$\Gamma_n(t_i^n):=y_i^n$ for $i=0,1,\dots,n$, and $\Gamma_n(t):=y_{i-1}^n$
if $t\in T\cap(t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n)$ and $i=1,\dots,n$. It remains to note
(for $T\subset[t_0,b]$) that
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_n,T)&=\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma_n,T\cap[t_{i-1}^n,t_i^n])
  =\sum_{i=1}^n d(y_{i-1}^n,y_i^n)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n d(y_{i-1}^n,F(t_i^n))\le\sum_{i=1}^n e(F(t_{i-1}^n),F(t_i^n))
  \le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{align*}
In this way, Theorem~\ref{t:BV} above is a generalization of \cite[Theorem~1]{JMAA07},
treating the existence of single-valued selectors on (connected) intervals $T\subset\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $X_0=\{x_0\}$ the construction yields a single-valued selector by picking one nearest point at each step; generalizes Chistyakov-Repovs.
nodes.label: r:single

nodes.name: Banach sequence space $\ell_1(\mathbb{N};\mathbb{B})$ for the examples
nodes.statement:
Let $(\mathbb{B},|\cdot|)$ be a Banach space with norm $|\cdot|$ (e.g.,
$\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{R}$), $\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of all sequences
$x:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{B}$, and $M=\ell_1(\mathbb{N};\mathbb{B})$ be the (infinite-dimensional)
Banach space of all \emph{summable\/} sequences $x\in\mathbb{B}^{\mathbb{N}}$ equipped
with the norm $\|x\|:=\sum_{i=1}^\infty|x(i)|<+\infty$ and, hence, metric
$d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ for $x,y\in M$.
nodes.statement_short: Examples take $M=\ell_1(\mathbb{N};\mathbb{B})$ with the $\ell_1$ norm metric.

nodes.name: Unit vectors $u_n$
nodes.statement:
Fix $u\in\mathbb{B}$ with $|u|=1$
(e.g., $u=1$ in $\mathbb{R}$) and, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, denote by $u_n$ the unit vector
in $M$ defined as usual by $u_n(i)=0$ if $i\ne n$, and $u_n(n)=u$.

nodes.name: Bounded closed values: selectors may fail to exist
nodes.statement:
A multifunction $F$ on $T\subset\mathbb{R}$ with (only) \emph{bounded closed\/} values
in $M$ and ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)<+\infty$ may have no set-valued selectors $\Gamma$ satisfying
  \begin{equation} \mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[t_0,+\infty)})\quad\mbox{or}
  \quad d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0))
  \end{equation}
with $t_0\in T$ and $X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$. In order to see this, we set
$T:=[0,1]$ and $X:=X_0\cup Y$, where $X_0:=\{u_1\}$ and
$Y:=\{\alpha_nu_n:n\ge2\}$ with $\alpha_n:=1+(1/n)$, and note that $X$ and $Y$
are bounded and closed (but not compact) subsets of $M$, whereas
$X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$ and $X_0\subset X$.
Define $F:T\to\{X,Y\}\subset\mathcal{P}(M)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ by
$F(0):=X$ and $F(t):=Y$ if $0<t\le1$. (A similar example was given in
\cite[Example~2]{JMAA} for $F$ with $\mbox{\rm V}(F,T)<+\infty$.) We have
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=e(X,Y)$, where
  \begin{align*}
e(X,Y)&=\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{y\in Y}d(x,y)=e(X\setminus Y,Y)=e(X_0,Y)\\
&=\inf_{n\ge2}(|u_1|+\alpha_n|u_n|)=1+\inf_{n\ge2}\Bigl(1+\frac1n\Bigr)=2.
  \end{align*}
Since $Y\subset X$, $F$ is nonincreasing on $T$ (Section~\ref{ss:mon}), and so,
${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$.

(a) Suppose $t_0=0$, so that $T_{[t_0,+\infty)}=T$. We have $X_0\subset X=F(0)$,
which implies $e(X_0,F(0))=0$. Let $\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$
be \emph{any\/} set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$ such that $\Gamma(0)=X_0$.
Since $\varnothing\ne\Gamma(1)\subset F(1)=Y$, $\alpha_nu_n\in\Gamma(1)$ for some
$n\ge2$. It follows that
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&\ge d_H(\Gamma(0),\Gamma(1))\ge e(\Gamma(1),\Gamma(0))
  =e(\Gamma(1),X_0)\\[1pt]
&\ge d(\alpha_nu_n,u_1)=\alpha_n+1>2={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{align*}

(b) Now, suppose $0<t_0\le1$, and $\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$
is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$. Since $\Gamma(t_0)\subset F(t_0)=Y$,
we have $\alpha_nu_n\in\Gamma(t_0)$ for some $n\ge2$, and so,
  \begin{align*}
d_H(X_0,\Gamma(t_0))&\ge e(\Gamma(t_0),X_0)\ge d(\alpha_nu_n,u_1)
  =\alpha_n+1\\[3pt]
&>2=e(X_0,Y)=e(X_0,F(t_0)).
  \end{align*}

(c) The effect of nonexistence of set-valued selectors in (a) and (b) above is due to
the fact that $\mbox{Pr}_YX_0=\varnothing$ (cf.~\mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Pr})}): indeed, if $y\in Y$, then
$y=\alpha_nu_n$ for some $n\ge2$, and so, for $x\in X_0=\{u_1\}$, we have
  \begin{equation*}
d(x,y)=d(u_1,\alpha_nu_n)=1+\alpha_n>2=e(X_0,Y)=d(u_1,Y)=d(x,Y).
  \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: A step multifunction with bounded closed non-compact values in $\ell_1$ has no selector satisfying the bounds of Theorem 1.
nodes.label: ex1

nodes.name: Non-compact value at a single point
nodes.statement:
This example is more subtle than Example~\ref{ex1}: even if $F(t)$ is bounded and
closed (but not compact) at a \emph{single\/} point $t\in T$, inequalities \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:zz})}
may not hold in Theorem~\ref{t:BV} (this is inspired by \cite[Example~5.2]{Sovae}).

Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$, $N\ge2$, be fixed and $\{\alpha_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\subset\mathbb{R}$ be
a sequence such that
  \begin{equation} \mbox{$\{|\alpha_n|\}_{n=1}^\infty$ \,is \,strictly \,decreasing}\quad
\mbox{and}\!\!\quad\inf_{n\ge N+1}|\alpha_n|>0
  \end{equation}
(e.g., $\alpha_n=\alpha(n+1)/n$ with $\alpha\ne0$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$). We set
$X:=\{\alpha_nu_n:1\le n\le N\}$ and $Y:=\{\alpha_nu_n:n\ge N+1\}$.
Clearly, $X\in\mbox{c}(M)$, while $Y\notin\mbox{c}(M)$ is bounded (by the first
condition in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:C1})}) and closed (by the second condition in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:C1})}) in $M$.
Define $F$ on $T:=[0,1]$ by $F(t)\!:=X$ if $0\le t<1$, and $F(1)\!:=Y$. We have
  \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=e(X,Y)=|\alpha_1|+\inf_{n\ge N+1}|\alpha_n|
  \end{equation*}
and
  \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=e(Y,X)=|\alpha_{N+1}|+|\alpha_N|.
  \end{equation*}

(a) Suppose $0\le t_0<1$ and $X_0:=\{\alpha_1u_1\}$, so that
$T_{[t_0,+\infty)}=[t_0,1]$ and $X_0\subset X=F(t_0)$, which implies
$e(X_0,F(t_0))=0$. Let $\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ be a
set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$ such that $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$. Since
$\Gamma(1)\subset F(1)=Y$, we find $\alpha_nu_n\in\Gamma(1)$ for some
$n\ge N+1$, and so,
  \begin{align*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,[t_0,1])&\ge d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(1))\ge e (\Gamma(1),X_0)
  \ge d(\alpha_nu_n,\alpha_1u_1)=|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_1|\\[2pt]
&>|\alpha_1|+\inf_{i\ge N+1}|\alpha_i|={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,[t_0,1]).
  \end{align*}

(b) Suppose $t_0=1$ and $X_0:=\{\alpha_1u_1\}$. If
$\Gamma:T\to\mathcal{P}(M)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ is a set-valued selector of $F$ on $T$,
then $\Gamma(1)\subset F(1)=Y$ implies $\alpha_nu_n\in\Gamma(1)$ for some
$n\ge N+1$, and so,
  \begin{align*}
d_H(X_0,\Gamma(1))&\ge e(\Gamma(1),X_0)\ge d(\alpha_nu_n,\alpha_1u_1)
  =|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_1|\\[2pt]
&>|\alpha_1|+\inf_{i\ge N+1}|\alpha_i|=e(X,Y)\ge e(X_0,Y)=e(X_0,F(t_0)).
  \end{align*}

(c) Clearly, $\mbox{Pr}_XX_0=X_0$. The non-existence of set-valued selectors in (a)
and (b) is again due to the fact that $\mbox{Pr}_YX_0=\varnothing$: in fact, if $y\in Y$,
then $y=\alpha_nu_n$ for some $n\ge N+1$, and so, we have,
for $x\in X_0=\{\alpha_1u_1\}$,
  \begin{equation*}
d(x,y)\!=\!d(\alpha_1u_1,\alpha_nu_n)\!=\!|\alpha_1|+|\alpha_n|
\!>\!\!\inf_{i\ge N+1}(|\alpha_1|+|\alpha_i|)\!=\!\inf_{y\in Y}d(x,y)\!=\!d(x,Y).
  \end{equation*}

(d) We claim that Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(b) holds with $t_0=1$ and $\Gamma(1)=X_0$
(except that $\Gamma(1)\in\mbox{c}(M)$) for every nonempty $X_0\subset Y=F(1)$.

First, observe that $\mbox{Pr}_XY_0=\{\alpha_Nu_N\}$ for every
$\varnothing\ne Y_0\subset Y$ (recall that $X\in\mbox{c}(M)$, and $\mbox{Pr}_XY_0$ is the
set of those $x\in X$, for which $d(y_0,x)=d(y_0,X)$ for some $y_0\in Y_0$).
To see this, we set $n_0:=\min\{n\ge N+1:\alpha_nu_n\in Y_0\}$ for $Y_0\subset Y$.
If $y_0\in Y_0$, we have $y_0=\alpha_nu_n$ for some $n\ge n_0$,
  \begin{equation*}
d(y_0,X)=\inf_{x\in X}d(y_0,x)=\min_{1\le i\le N}(|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_i|)
  =|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_N|,\\[2pt]
  \end{equation*}
and
  \begin{equation*}
\mbox{$d(y_0,x)=|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_i|$ \,if \,$x=\alpha_iu_i\in X$ for some $1\le i\le N$.}
  \end{equation*}
If $n=n_0$ and $i=N$, we find $y_0=\alpha_{n_0}u_{n_0}\in Y_0$,
$x=\alpha_Nu_N\in X$, and
  \begin{equation*}
d(y_0,x)=d(\alpha_{n_0}u_{n_0},\alpha_Nu_N)=|\alpha_{n_0}|+|\alpha_N|=d(y_0,X),
  \end{equation*}
which implies $\alpha_Nu_N\in\mbox{Pr}_XY_0$. Now, if $i<N$, then
$|\alpha_i|>|\alpha_N|$, and so, for every $y_0\in Y_0$, we get
  \begin{equation*}
d(y_0,x)=|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_i|>|\alpha_n|+|\alpha_N|=d(y_0,X).
  \end{equation*}
Thus, $\alpha_iu_i\notin\mbox{Pr}_XY_0$ for all $i=1,\dots,N-1$, and we are through.

Taking the above into account, define a set-valued selector $\Gamma$ of $F$ on $T$
by $\Gamma(t):=\{\alpha_Nu_N\}$ if $0\le t<1$, and $\Gamma(1):=X_0$ with
$X_0=Y_0\subset Y$. It remains to note that $n_0\ge N+1$ implies
  \begin{align*}
{\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(\Gamma,T)&=e(Y_0,\{\alpha_Nu_N\})=\sup_{y_0\in Y_0}d(y_0,\alpha_Nu_N)
  =|\alpha_{n_0}|+|\alpha_N|\\
&\le|\alpha_{N+1}|+|\alpha_N|={\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T).
  \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Non-compactness at a single point already breaks the bounds of Theorem 1(a), while 1(b) still holds.
nodes.label: ex2

nodes.name: Finite right variation with infinite left variation
nodes.statement_short: A nondecreasing compact-valued $F$ on $[0,1]$ with $\overrightarrow{V}=0$ and $\overleftarrow{V}=\infty$: Theorem 1(a) applies, Theorem A does not.
nodes.label: ex3

nodes.name: Necessity of the initial point and of the jump term
nodes.statement:
(a) By Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a), given $X_0\in\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$X_0\subset X_1=F(0)$, multifunction $F$ from Example~\ref{ex3} has a constant
set-valued selector $\Gamma:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ satisfying $\Gamma(0)=X_0$
and $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$. However, if $0<t_0\le1$ and $X_0\subset F(t_0)$,
there may be no set-valued selector $\Gamma$ of $F$ on $T$ such that
$\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$ and $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)$. In fact, let $t_0=\tau_n$
for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (cf. Example~\ref{ex3}), so that $F(t_0)=F(\tau_n)=X_{n+1}$.
Suppose now that $X_0\subset X_{n+1}\setminus X_1\subset F(t_0)$,
$\Gamma(t)\subset F(t)$ for all $t\in T$, and $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$. Since
$\Gamma(0)\subset F(0)=X_1$, we have $\alpha_iu_i\in\Gamma(0)$ for some
$1\le i\le N$, or $0\in\Gamma(0)$ (i.e., possibly, $\alpha_i=0$), and so,
  \begin{align}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T)&\ge d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(0))=d_H(X_0,\Gamma(0))
  \ge e(\Gamma(0),X_0)\nonumber\\[3pt]
&\ge d(\alpha_iu_i,X_0)\ge d(\alpha_iu_i,X_{n+1}\setminus X_1)\nonumber\\[2pt]
&=\min_{N+1\le k\le (n+1)N}(\alpha_i+\alpha_k)\ge\alpha_{(n+1)N}
  >0={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T). \end{align}

(b) If $t_0>a=\inf T$ and $\Gamma(t_0)=X_0$, inequality
$\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0)})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0)})$ in Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a) cannot
in general be replaced by $\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,T_{[a,t_0]})\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T_{[a,t_0]})$.
This can be seen from Example~\ref{ex4} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:519})}:
  \begin{equation*}
\mbox{\rm V}(\Gamma,[0,t_0])\ge d_H(\Gamma(t_0),\Gamma(0))\ge\dots\ge
\alpha_{(n+1)N}>0={\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,[0,t_0]).
  \end{equation*}
This observation also makes it explicit that the ``jump'' $J_a(\Gamma,t_0)$ is
essential  in the left-hand side of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:s1t0})}.
nodes.statement_short: For $t_0>\inf T$ a selector through $X_0$ may need variation exceeding $\overrightarrow{V}(F,T)$; the jump $J_a$ is essential.
nodes.label: ex4

nodes.name: Image not totally bounded under bounded right variation
nodes.statement:
This example is designed for Remark~\ref{p:7}. Let $T:=[1,+\infty)$ and
$F:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ be given by $F(t)\!:=\!X_n$ if $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n\le t<n+1$,
where $X_n\!:=\!\{u_i:1\le i\le n\}$. We have $X_n\in\mbox{c}(M)$, and
$F(s)\subset F(t)$ for all $1\le s\le t<+\infty$, and so, ${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=0$. The image
\mbox{$F(T)=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty X_n=\{u_i:i\in\mathbb{N}\}$} is bounded in $M$,
but \emph{not\/} totally bounded (i.e., cannot be covered by a finite number of balls
of arbitrarily small radius). Note that ${\scriptstyle\overleftarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F,T)=+\infty$ (consider a partition
$1<2<\dots<m-1<m$ of $T$ with arbitrary $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and observe that
$e(X_{n+1},X_n)=2$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$). This example is easily adapted to the case
when $F$ maps $[a,b)$ or $[a,b]$ into~$\mbox{c}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Nondecreasing $F$ on $[1,\infty)$ with $\overrightarrow{V}=0$ whose image is bounded but not totally bounded.
nodes.label: ex:5.5

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (functional inclusion $X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$)
nodes.statement_short: Parametrized Banach contraction: under a directional variation bound, a uniform contraction and a compact envelope, $X(t)\subset F(t,X(t))$ has a BV solution with initial condition.
assumptions: there is a nondecreasing bounded function $\varphi:T\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
there is a number $0\le\mu<1$ such that
there is a multifunction $K:T\to\mbox{\rm c}(M)$ such that
$t_0:=\inf T\in T$ and $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
if $X_0\subset F(t_0,X_0)$
$t_0:=\inf T\in T$ and $X_0\in\mbox{\rm c}(M)$
if $X_0\subset F(t_0,X_0)$

nodes.label: t:FuEm

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
First, observe that assumptions (a) and (b) and the triangle inequality for $e$ imply,
for all $s,t\in T$, $s\le t$, and $X,Y\in\mbox{c}(M)$,
  \begin{equation} e(F(s,X),F(t,Y))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)+\mu d_H(X,Y).
  \end{equation}

We set $X_0(t)\!:=\!X_0$ and $F_0(t)\!:=\!F(t,X_0)$ for $t\in T$. We have
\mbox{$F_0:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$}, and assumption (a) and Lemma~\ref{l:char} imply
${\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_0,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)<+\infty$. By Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a), there is
$X_1\equiv\Gamma:T=T_{[t_0,+\infty)}\to\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$X_1(t)\subset F_0(t)$ for all $t\in T$, $d_H(X_0,X_1(t_0))\le e(X_0,F_0(t_0))$, and
$\mbox{\rm V}(X_1,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_0,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)$. In what follows we apply the standard
iteration procedure. Setting $F_1(t):=F(t,X_1(t))$ for $t\in T$, we find
$F_1:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ and, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:XY})},
  \begin{equation*}
e(F_1(s),F_1(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)+\mu d_H(X_1(s),X_1(t))\quad
  \forall\,s,t\in T,\,\,s\le t.
  \end{equation*}
Arguing with partitions of $T$, Lemma~\ref{l:char} implies
  \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_1,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)+\mu\mbox{\rm V}(X_1,T)\le(1+\mu)\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T).
  \end{equation*}
Applying Theorem~\ref{t:BV} again, we obtain $X_2:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ such that
$X_2(t)\subset F_1(t)$ for all $t\in T$, $d_H(X_0,X_2(t_0))\le e(X_0,F_1(t_0))$, and
  \begin{equation*}
\mbox{\rm V}(X_2,T)\le{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_1,T)\le(1+\mu)\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T).
  \end{equation*}
If $F_2(t)\!:=\!F(t,X_2(t))$, $t\in T$, then $F_2:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ and, by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:XY})},
  \begin{equation*}
e(F_2(s),F_2(t))\le\varphi(t)-\varphi(s)+\mu d_H(X_2(s),X_2(t))\quad
  \forall\,s,t\in T,\,\,s\le t,
  \end{equation*}
and so,
  \begin{equation*}
{\scriptstyle\overrightarrow{\mbox{\rm V}}}(F_2,T)\le\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)+\mu\mbox{\rm V}(X_2,T)\le(1+\mu+\mu^2)\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T).
  \end{equation*}

Arguing by induction, we obtain the sequence $\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of multifunctions
$X_n:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$ such that, given $n\in\mathbb{N}$,
  \begin{eqnarray}
&X_n(t)\subset F_{n-1}(t)\!:=\!F(t,X_{n-1}(t))\subset K(t)\quad\mbox{for all $t\in T$,}& \\[3pt]
&d_H(X_0,X_n(t_0))\le e(X_0,F_{n-1}(t_0))\!=\!e\bigl(X_0,F(t_0,X_{n-1}(t_0))\bigr),
  \,\,\mbox{and}& \\
&\displaystyle\mbox{\rm V}(X_n,T)\le\biggl(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mu^i\biggr)\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)
  \le\frac1{1-\mu}\,\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T).& \end{eqnarray}
By \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vft})}, the sequence $\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is of uniformly bounded Jordan
variation with respect to $d_H$, and so, condition (a) in Theorem~\ref{t:B} is satisfied,
and by \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xnt})}, the closure $\ov{\{X_n(t):n\in\mathbb{N}\}}$ in $\mbox{c}(M)$ is compact
for every $t\in T$, and so, condition (b) in Theorem~\ref{t:B} is fulfiled.
By Theorem~\ref{t:B}, a subsequence of $\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, again denoted by
$\{X_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$, converges in $\mbox{c}(M)$ pointwise on $T$ to a
multifunction $X:T\to\mbox{c}(M)$, i.e., $d_H(X_n(t),X(t))\to0$ as $n\to\infty$
for all $t\in T$.

We are going to verify that $X$ satisfies assertions (i), (ii), and (iii). Assertion (i)
is a consequence of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vft})} and the lower semicontinuity \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Vsem})} of~$\mbox{\rm V}$.
In order to see that (ii) holds, we make use of the following inequality
(cf. \cite[inequality~(11.7)]{Sovae}), which is valid for all $X,X',Y,Y'\in\mbox{c}(M)$:
  \begin{equation} |e(X,Y)-e(X',Y')|\le d_H(X,X')+d_H(Y,Y').
  \end{equation}
In fact, given $t\in T$, \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Xnt})} implies $e\bigl(X_n(t),F(t,X_{n-1}(t))\bigr)=0$,
and so, taking into account \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Sog})} and \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:XY})}, we get
  \begin{align*}
e(X(t),F(t,X(t)))&\!=\!\bigl|e(X(t),F(t,X(t)))\!-\!e(X_n(t),F(t,X_{n-1}(t)))\bigr|\\[2pt]
&\!\le\! d_H(X(t),X_n(t))\!+\!d_H(F(t,X(t)),F(t,X_{n-1}(t)))\\[2pt]
&\!\le\! d_H(X(t),X_n(t))\!+\!\mu d_H(X(t),X_{n-1}(t))\to0
  \,\,\,\,\mbox{as}\,\,\,n\to\infty.
  \end{align*}
Thus, $e(X(t),F(t,X(t)))=0$, which implies (by properties of~$e$) assertion~(ii).

To establish (iii), we note that (cf. \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Hot})} and (iii))
  \begin{equation*}
|d_H(X_0,X_n(t_0))-d_H(X_0,X(t_0))|\le d_H(X_n(t_0),X(t_0))\to0
  \,\,\,\,\mbox{as}\,\,\,n\to\infty,
  \end{equation*}
and, by virtue of \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Sog})} and assumption (b),
  \begin{align*}
&\qquad\bigl|e(X_0,F(t_0,X_{n-1}(t_0)))-e(X_0,F(t_0,X(t_0)))\bigr|\\[2pt]
\le&\,d_H(F(t_0,X_{n-1}(t_0)),F(t_0,X(t_0)))\le\mu d_H(X_{n-1}(t_0),X(t_0))
  \to0,\,\,n\to\infty.
  \end{align*}
Passing to the limit as $n\to\infty$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Hot})}, we arrive at~(iii).

Finally, suppose $X_0\!\subset\! F(t_0,X_0)$. Hence $X_0\!\subset\! F_0(t_0)$ and
$e(X_0,F_0(t_0))\!=\!0$. From the above,
$d_H(X_0,X_1(t_0))\!\le\! e(X_0,F_0(t_0))\!=\!0$,
and so, $X_1(t_0)\!=\!X_0$. Since
  \begin{equation*}
X_0\subset F_0(t_0)=F(t_0,X_0)=F(t_0,X_1(t_0))=F_1(t_0),
  \end{equation*}
we find from $d_H(X_0,X_2(t_0))\le e(X_0,F_1(t_0))=0$ that $X_2(t_0)=X_0$.
By induction, we deduce from \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Hot})} that $X_n(t_0)=X_0$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
Passing to the lmit as $n\to\infty$ in \mbox{\rm(\ref{e:Hot})}, we get
$d_H(X_0,X(t_0))\le e(X_0,F(t_0,X_0))=0$, which yields $X(t_0)=X_0$.
\qed
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Theorem 1(a) on $F(t,X_{n-1}(t))$ to get uniformly BV approximations, extract a pointwise limit by Theorem B, and pass to the limit using the contraction.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 versus Theorem 1 and Banach's Contraction Theorem
nodes.statement:
If $F(t,X)=F(t)$ is independent of $X\in\mbox{c}(M)$ (or $\mu=0$), Theorem~
\ref{t:FuEm} gives back Theorem~\ref{t:BV}(a): we may set $\varphi=\ori{v}_{F}$
and~$K=F$. On the other hand, if $F(t,X)=F(X)$ is independent of $t\in T$ (or
$\varphi\equiv0$), Theorem~\ref{t:FuEm} is a consequence of Banach's Contraction
Theorem (in fact, $F:\mbox{c}(K)\to\mbox{c}(K)$ is a contraction on compact,
hence complete, metric space $(\mbox{c}(K),d_H)$ with $K=K(t_0)$).
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2 reduces to Theorem 1(a) when $F$ ignores $X$, and to Banach's contraction theorem on $(c(K),d_H)$ when $F$ ignores $t$.

nodes.name: Scaled multifunction satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: $F(t,X)=\varphi_0(t)X$ with nondecreasing $\varphi_0<1$ satisfies conditions (a)-(c) of Theorem 2.
nodes.label: ex:6.1

nodes.name: Cantor-type solutions of a functional inclusion
nodes.statement:
In Example~\ref{ex:6.1}, we set $\mathbb{B}:=\mathbb{R}$, $K:=[0,1]$, and
$\varphi_0(t):=t$ for $t\in T:=[0,1/2]$ (hence $\mu=1/2$, $\varphi=\varphi_0$,
and $\mbox{\rm V}(\varphi,T)=1/2$). Define $F$ by
  \begin{equation*}
F(t,X):=(tX)\cup(1-t+tX),\quad t\in T,\,\,X\in\mbox{c}(K).
  \end{equation*}
For instance, if $X=[0,1]$, we have $F(0,X)=\{0,1\}$, $F(1/2,X)=[0,1]$, and if
$0<t<1/2$, then $F(t,X)=[0,t]\cup[1-t,1]$, $F(t,[0,t])=[0,t^2]\cup[1-t,1-t+t^2]$,
$F(t,[1-t,1])=[t-t^2,t]\cup[1-t^2,1]$, and so on. The iterative construction of the
classical Cantor (ternary) set corresponds to $t=1/3$ (e.g., \cite[p.~20]{GK}).

By Theorem~\ref{t:FuEm}, there is $X:[0,1/2]\to\mbox{c}([0,1])$ such that
$\mbox{\rm V}(X,[0,1/2])\!\le\!1$, $X(t)\subset(tX(t))\cup(1-t+tX(t))$ for all $t\in[0,1/2]$, and
$X(0)=\{0,1\}$. For every $t\in(0,1/2)$, the compact set $X(t)\subset[0,1]$ is a
Cantor-type perfect set.
nodes.statement_short: $F(t,X)=(tX)\cup(1-t+tX)$ on $[0,1/2]$ yields BV solutions $X(t)$ that are Cantor-type perfect sets.
